questions.title: Establish the missing review ground truth
questions.stem: A mediation assistant must identify disputed obligations in agreements. Historical files contain final settlements but no obligation labels; reviewers disagree on those labels. The pilot needs evaluation before public use. What BEST establishes feasibility beyond having thousands of documents?

options.text: Agree labels with reviewers and adjudicate a representative sample for a bounded pilot evaluation.
options.why: This addresses missing task ground truth and review consistency, turning an attractive language task into an assessable pilot rather than assuming raw documents prove fit.

options.text: Launch with the full corpus; settle labels after public users reveal which answers help.
options.why: Public helpfulness cannot replace the required pre-use evaluation and leaves the unresolved label policy to emerge after users have already relied on outputs.

options.text: Derive obligation labels from settlement amounts, treating each completed mediation as evidence of disputed clauses.
options.why: Settlement amounts do not identify disputed clauses or their reasons, so the proposed proxy creates labels that the available records do not actually support.

options.text: Compare model tiers by supported agreement length, using corpus capacity as evidence of task feasibility.
options.why: Capacity to accept long text does not establish correct obligation labels or consistent review, which are the missing prerequisites for evaluating this language task.

questions.decision: Resolve the task definition with reviewers and create an adjudicated reference sample before claiming pilot feasibility. The material is language-heavy, but available documents are not automatically usable evaluation evidence. This is a novel application of the chapter’s fit check: uncertainty about labels and review consistency is a prerequisite to investigate, not a reason to treat raw volume as proof.

video_evidence.concept: Language-heavy work with available evidence and accountable review supports an LLM fit check.

questions.title: Requirements before topology
questions.stem: A repair network needs shift briefings from work orders. Quality criteria and budget are approved, but briefing deadlines and permitted processing locations remain undefined. Architects propose either one call or several specialists. Which TWO decisions establish measurable constraints before choosing?

options.text: Define permitted processing locations and transfers for restricted orders, with an owner confirming eligibility.
options.why: The allowed processing boundary constrains deployment options independently of whether the application uses one call or several specialist workers.

options.text: Set a start-to-usable-briefing deadline at specified shift-change load, counting incomplete briefings against the target.
options.why: A deadline tied to a workload and outcome gives both candidate topologies an observable timing acceptance criterion rather than an architectural preference.

options.text: Set the maximum specialist count and use that limit as the briefing service's latency requirement.
options.why: Worker count is an implementation decision and does not specify the experienced deadline or prove that a particular topology meets it.

options.text: Standardize vector database and SDK versions, treating those dependencies as the service's operating envelope.
options.why: Standardized components can simplify implementation, but their versions do not define the load, elapsed-time target, or authorized geographic processing boundaries.

options.text: Replace the quality rubric with unanimous architecture-team approval that briefings sound decisive and polished.
options.why: This discards an existing quality contract and supplies neither a measurable timing requirement nor a defined data-processing boundary.

questions.decision: Agree observable timing and data-processing boundaries before choosing a topology. These constrain any model, orchestration, and deployment route. The quality rubric and budget already exist; repeating component preferences cannot fill missing service requirements. Their owners should define acceptance measurements so proposed architectures can be compared consistently.

video_evidence.concept: Non-functional requirements describe measurable constraints rather than implementation choices.

questions.title: Validate the serialized artifact
questions.stem: A radio gateway requires UTF-8 payloads of at most 240 bytes and an allowlisted incident code. Accented names exceed the byte limit; truncating the code risks misrouting. Retries cost money. One rewrite is allowed before dispatcher takeover. Which design BEST enforces delivery?

options.text: Check incoming reports against 240 bytes, then allow unrestricted drafts from inputs that pass.
options.why: Input size does not constrain generated output, and this rejects potentially useful source reports without enforcing the actual delivery boundary.

options.text: Check encoded length and code before sending; allow one rewrite, then escalate remaining failures.
options.why: This checks the actual transport artifact and preserves the code's routing meaning while providing a bounded recovery path for invalid drafts.

options.text: Truncate drafts to 240 bytes before sending, retaining the incident-code characters that still fit.
options.why: Truncation enforces size while risking code corruption and meaning loss; the contract requires a valid incident code as well as a bounded payload.

options.text: Instruct 240-character drafts and retry rejected deliveries, treating character compliance as sufficient for UTF-8.
options.why: UTF-8 characters can occupy multiple bytes, so this instruction misses the demonstrated failure and charged retries cannot repair an invalid payload.

questions.decision: Validate the exact serialized output at the last pre-delivery boundary. Byte length differs from character count, and the code has routing semantics that truncation can corrupt. A bounded rewrite followed by the same validation preserves useful generation while preventing an invalid artifact from reaching the gateway.

video_evidence.concept: Output validation belongs between generation and delivery and must enforce the channel contract.

questions.title: Refresh the field that changed
questions.stem: A seat assistant has a current seating catalogue but suggests seats another buyer holds. A separate inventory service supplies authoritative request-time status. Suggestions need not guarantee purchase, but must reflect inventory observed for that request. Which change BEST fixes context assembly?

options.text: Fetch candidate-seat inventory with observation times; use it for suggestions and recheck reservations at purchase.
options.why: The stale field is availability, so its live authority must supply the context; a later reservation boundary remains necessary as inventory can change.

options.text: Refresh the catalogue per request; use its current descriptions to validate yesterday's availability snapshot.
options.why: The catalogue and inventory have distinct authority, so refreshing descriptions cannot establish whether another buyer currently holds the suggested seats.

options.text: Keep the snapshot but train tentative wording, omitting timestamps so suggestions avoid implying certainty.
options.why: Uncertainty wording does not meet the requirement that suggestions reflect inventory observed for the current request, and omitting time conceals the evidence gap.

options.text: Validate against the static catalogue before answering, keeping inventory lookups outside the request path.
options.why: A validator cannot infer live inventory from a catalogue that lacks that field; it needs authoritative current state rather than another processing stage.

questions.decision: Refresh availability from its own authoritative service and retain the observation time with the selected seats. Catalogue freshness does not establish inventory freshness. The model can explain the observed options, but the final purchase still needs its separate reservation check because suggestions are not a guarantee of later availability.

video_evidence.concept: Assemble current authoritative state at request time for changing operational facts.

questions.title: Discover dependencies in a branching investigation
questions.stem: A publisher investigates a photographer's aliases across collections. Searches can reveal more aliases. Specialists may propose collection-specific corrections but cannot edit records; a final editor reconciles them. Which TWO choices support controlled orchestrator-worker discovery?

options.text: Run five full-corpus investigations; select the majority correction list without collection provenance or task ownership.
options.why: Whole-task voting can increase confidence in some settings, but it does not supply controlled discovery, scoped workers, or evidence needed to reconcile distinct corrections.

options.text: Route each known alias separately; discard newly discovered aliases when reconciling the correction packages.
options.why: Fixed initial routes assume the unknown aliases away and can lose the very evidence that makes this investigation require dynamic decomposition.

options.text: Schedule every collection upfront; finish them all before investigating any aliases discovered during searches.
options.why: This replaces evidence-driven decomposition with exhaustive fixed work and delays relevant discoveries without meeting the stated need for adaptable investigation.

options.text: Require correction proposals, source references, and unresolved leads within a job-wide limit on further expansion.
options.why: Bounded result contracts support synthesis and controlled dynamic discovery without granting workers shared-record editing authority or an unlimited investigation budget.

options.text: Maintain a deduplicated registry of discovered aliases and collections; create scoped tasks as evidence emerges.
options.why: The actual task graph emerges from evidence, and a registry prevents repeated discoveries from silently creating duplicate or uncontrolled investigation work.

questions.decision: Use dynamic discovery to create collection-scoped work, then synthesize bounded proposals with an explicit completion policy. This is a novel extension of the chapter's pattern: unknown work justifies orchestration, while a registry and limits make it operationally manageable. Fixed routes and repeated whole-task answers do not discover the changing work graph.

video_evidence.concept: Orchestrator-workers suits subtasks whose number and nature emerge from analysis.

questions.title: Choose a threshold from observed votes
questions.stem: An inspection assistant runs three independent image reviews. Flags trigger technician review, never maintenance. The representative replay below deduplicates flags. The owner requires ≥90% defect detection and ≤100 reviews daily. Which aggregation rule meets both gates on this evidence?

options.text: Use one pass, assigning it the two-vote results because the model and images are unchanged.
options.why: The table measures aggregated three-pass policies; it supplies no basis for assigning those detection and workload figures to a different single-pass system.

options.text: Require all three flags: its smaller queue allows technicians to inspect flagged items more carefully.
options.why: Unanimity reduces workload to 58 reviews but detects only 83% of defects, below the owner's explicit floor regardless of later review depth.

options.text: Require at least two flags: observed detection is 91% and daily review load is 94.
options.why: Both independent acceptance gates hold for this replay; the other thresholds each violate one constraint despite offering a legitimate benefit on the other.

options.text: Escalate any flag: its measured detection advantage takes precedence over the daily technician-review ceiling.
options.why: Any-flag improves recall but generates 142 reviews, exceeding the available capacity; a stronger value on one metric cannot waive another required gate.

questions.decision: Choose the threshold that meets both observed gates. Any-flag finds more defects but exceeds review capacity; unanimity fits capacity but misses the detection floor. The two-vote rule gives 91% detection and 94 reviews. This measured threshold decision extends the chapter's recall-oriented voting lesson without making independence a performance guarantee.

video_evidence.concept: Parallel voting thresholds trade missed findings against false flags and must match error costs.

questions.title: Read-only means the underlying credential too
questions.stem: A diagnostic worker's only tool, inspect_asset, forwards arbitrary API paths using the repair worker's credential. A red-team call reaches a write endpoint. Diagnostics need asset-condition data. Which TWO changes restore the role boundary?

options.text: Replace path forwarding with asset reads accepting validated identifiers and returning only required condition fields.
options.why: The wrapper can no longer route model-supplied paths to unrelated API operations, which removes the hidden write path while preserving diagnostics.

options.text: Give diagnostics an upstream credential permitting required reads but excluding repair and update endpoints.
options.why: Independent upstream least privilege limits the worker's authority even if a wrapper defect later permits an unexpected request path.

options.text: Have the lead summarize completed diagnostic calls, retaining the shared credential and arbitrary-path interface.
options.why: Post-call summaries provide audit information after the side effect; they do not withdraw the capability that violates the role boundary.

options.text: Isolate diagnostics in another conversation while retaining its wrapper, path parameter, and repair-capable credential.
options.why: Conversation isolation separates context but leaves the same external authority intact, so the same write endpoint remains reachable through the tool.

options.text: Rename the tool read_only_inspect_asset and instruct the worker to supply only read-operation paths.
options.why: A clearer label can help selection, but arbitrary forwarding and a write-capable credential still make the demonstrated state-changing operation reachable.

questions.decision: Agent-specific tool names are insufficient if a tool hides broader authority. Constrain both the exposed operation and its underlying credential to diagnostic reads. This extends the chapter's least-privilege lesson through the wrapper boundary: authority depends on reachable behavior, not the name shown to the worker.

video_evidence.concept: Scope each agent to capabilities required by its role.

questions.title: Unknown is a result state
questions.stem: A groundwater report combines five labs. One instrument fails; downstream code turns its blank cell into zero contamination. Publication may disclose missing samples, but cannot call them clean. Successful labs must not rerun. Which design BEST preserves usable evidence?

options.text: Rerun all five labs after the deadline; publish the current report as complete pending retry.
options.why: A future retry does not justify present completeness and rerunning successful labs violates the explicit reuse requirement without addressing the current semantic error.

options.text: Remove the failed lab's row and denominator, publishing only samples whose results contain numbers.
options.why: Dropping the row conceals missing coverage and changes the apparent tested population; the deadline permits disclosed gaps, not silent denominator changes.

options.text: Keep blank cells and request cautious narrative, while leaving empty-to-zero calculation behavior in place.
options.why: The deterministic conversion still destroys the distinction before generation; cautious language cannot restore the original measurement state once it has been collapsed.

options.text: Carry typed sample states and provenance; exclude failures from calculations and enumerate samples lacking evidence.
options.why: This retains successful measurements and carries the failure into both calculations and narrative, preventing absent evidence from acquiring the meaning of measured zero.

questions.decision: Missing evidence must remain distinct from a measured zero. Use typed states and preserve sample scope through the aggregation path, then render the gap explicitly. The chapter's error-propagation lesson extends here to a domain-specific null-state error: carrying an error string is insufficient if downstream tables convert it into a numeric value.

video_evidence.concept: Workers must propagate explicit success, partial, and failure states into synthesis.

questions.title: Fixed stages with explicit skip evidence
questions.stem: Records migration must run identification, ownership validation, conversion, then reconciliation. Compatible records need no conversion, but auditors require evidence that conversion evaluated them and deliberately skipped work. Which design BEST preserves this contract?

options.text: Let a planner omit conversion for compatible records and log only stages it chooses to invoke.
options.why: Omitted stages leave no required evaluation evidence, and a planner's chosen path changes a workflow whose mandatory stage order is already known.

options.text: Combine the stages in one call and use its explanation as evidence of ordered execution.
options.why: A final explanation cannot establish separate ordered execution or intermediate stage results, so it does not meet the stated audit requirement.

options.text: Run stages concurrently, then sort saved results into the required order for the audit record.
options.why: Display order does not enforce execution dependencies; conversion and reconciliation could operate before identity and ownership validation establish their required inputs.

options.text: Keep the ordered stages; record conversion or reasoned skip, plus each stage's input version and result.
options.why: Explicit skip outcomes retain audit coverage and ordered dependencies without requiring a conversion that the record's validated state does not need.

questions.decision: Keep the prescribed stage graph and model optional work as an explicit stage result. A skipped conversion is a decision with evidence, not an absent stage. The workflow remains auditable and predictable while allowing language assistance inside bounded steps where interpretation is needed; dynamic stage invention adds no demonstrated value.

video_evidence.concept: Fixed decomposition supports known ordered checks and retained intermediate outputs.

questions.title: Normalize productivity for changing staffing
questions.stem: A translation unit measures productivity as accepted notes per paid editor hour. The matched workloads below use identical quality criteria, and paid hours include corrections. Output rose alongside overtime. Which conclusion correctly evaluates the productivity claim?

options.text: Productivity fell: paid editor hours increased, despite the matching proportional increase in accepted output.
options.why: Higher labor input alone cannot establish lower productivity; the correct ratio considers accepted output and paid time together in each period.

options.text: Throughput rose, but productivity stayed at three notes per paid hour; investigate other benefits.
options.why: Both periods have the same accepted-output-to-paid-time ratio, so the higher output does not establish an efficiency gain under the sponsor's definition.

options.text: Productivity rose about 22%: accepted notes increased from 960 to 1,170 under unchanged quality criteria.
options.why: This calculates throughput growth but omits the proportional increase in paid editor hours that the stated productivity denominator requires.

options.text: Productivity remains unmeasurable until token prices are known and replace editor hours in its denominator.
options.why: Token cost belongs in an economic assessment but does not replace the explicitly specified paid-hour denominator for this productivity measurement.

questions.decision: Normalize accepted work by the specified labor denominator. Before: 960/320 = 3 notes per paid hour. After: 1,170/390 = 3, so throughput rose 21.875% alongside hours, but measured productivity did not improve. The assistant may offer other value; this evidence alone does not support the claimed productivity gain.

video_evidence.concept: Productivity means output per person or unit of work time, distinct from cost and service latency.

questions.title: Attach savings to a quality gate
questions.stem: A cheaper routing configuration cuts inference spending from 800 to 260 units monthly. Aggregate accuracy passes, but rare-language accuracy falls to 88% against a mandatory, non-waivable 92% floor. Which TWO statements belong in the approval decision record?

options.text: Record 67.5% potential inference savings alongside the failed rare-language floor and current nonapproval decision.
options.why: The arithmetic accurately describes potential savings while preserving the owner's binding quality requirement rather than presenting savings as an unconditional release benefit.

options.text: Record 67.5% total operating savings, without further measurement of support or reviewer costs after adoption.
options.why: The evidence covers inference alone; extending its percentage to total operating expense silently assumes unmeasured cost categories fell at the same rate.

options.text: Require evaluated remediation or routing that meets the floor before claiming a deployable cost-quality trade-off.
options.why: A different complete configuration may become feasible, but its own measured quality and cost must support approval instead of inheriting the rejected candidate's claims.

options.text: Approve with a quality disclaimer: aggregate success compensates for the floor failure on infrequent documents.
options.why: A disclaimer and aggregate result do not waive a mandatory slice-specific requirement, even when the slice represents a small proportion of traffic.

options.text: Use aggregate accuracy in the record while retaining the rare-language floor in the owner's specification.
options.why: This creates inconsistent records and obscures a failed requirement; approval needs an authorized requirement change or a configuration that actually meets it.

questions.decision: The measured inference reduction is (800−260)/800 = 67.5%, but the candidate is ineligible under the current rare-language floor. Record both facts and require an evaluated remediation or scoped routing policy before approval. A business-value pillar supports transparent trade-offs, not using aggregate success to hide a failed binding constraint.

video_evidence.concept: Business-value decisions must state both measured savings and the accepted quality trade-off.

questions.title: A baseline is a measurement instrument
questions.stem: A coding team can evaluate one initial configuration. Its refactor and tool-driven debugging workload lacks acceptance tests. Provider guidance suggests a balanced tier as a starting candidate. Which approach BEST turns that recommendation into workload evidence?

options.text: Choose the cheapest tier permanently; extra attempts funded by its low price can offset task failures.
options.why: More attempts can increase cost and repeat errors; the proposed selection lacks evidence that the complete configuration meets the required task outcomes.

options.text: Define task checks; test the balanced tier with fixed tools and settings, using failures to guide comparisons.
options.why: A controlled baseline creates task evidence and supports informed expansion without assuming that the recommended starting tier automatically satisfies local requirements.

options.text: Optimize tools separately for each candidate, then attribute every measured difference exclusively to model family.
options.why: Different tools change the tested system, so the comparison cannot isolate the model and its results cannot be explained solely through model-family choice.

options.text: Deploy the strongest tier first; derive acceptance criteria later from users' preferences among generated patches.
options.why: Preference after deployment does not establish the required correctness bar, and capability branding cannot replace a controlled task acceptance baseline.

questions.decision: Use the balanced tier to establish a reproducible task baseline, not to preapprove production quality. Define checks and collect failed-task evidence before considering stronger or cheaper configurations. The chapter supplies a starting heuristic; this scenario deliberately avoids a permanent model-name claim and makes workload-specific evaluation the deciding evidence.

video_evidence.concept: A balanced production model is a starting hypothesis; evaluations determine the eventual model selection.

questions.title: Compare costs inside the eligible set
questions.stem: Daily usage is six million input and 0.4 million output tokens. Fictional rates and measured results appear below. Release gates are ≥94% accepted answers and p95 ≤2.5 seconds. With no caching, retries, or fixed charges, which eligible candidate costs least?

options.text: Choose C at 28.8 units daily; its excess accuracy justifies higher cost after both gates pass.
options.why: C is eligible but the question supplies no value for excess accuracy that overrides minimizing cost among configurations already satisfying both gates.

options.text: Choose B at 14.4 units daily; both gates pass, and the other eligible candidate costs more.
options.why: Its 94.5% quality and 2.3-second p95 pass, and applying both token categories produces the lowest eligible daily total.

options.text: Choose A at 2.1 units daily; its lower expense justifies tolerating 92% acceptance on this workload.
options.why: A is cheapest but fails the nonnegotiable 94% quality gate, so its cost cannot justify selection under the stated acceptance contract.

options.text: Choose B at 10.8 units daily; acceptance already reflects output quality, so omit output-token charges.
options.why: The rate schedule charges output tokens independently, and a quality measure does not remove those charges from the daily inference calculation.

questions.decision: B is the cheapest eligible configuration: 6×1.8 + 0.4×9 = 14.4 units daily. A costs 2.1 but fails quality. C costs 28.8 and meets both gates, so B wins the specified cost comparison. Fictional rates make this an arithmetic and feasibility decision rather than a current-price memorization task.

video_evidence.concept: Choose an evaluated model using quality requirements and complete input/output economics.

questions.title: Separate three meanings in a template
questions.stem: A warranty template mixes current corporate rules, fictional examples using obsolete policies, and supplier bulletins quoting old procedures. Maintainers must retain that evidence while applying current policy. Which THREE changes clarify authority, recognizing that formatting cannot enforce downstream authorization?

options.text: Put corporate rules in a supplier-bulletin appendix, giving all relevant text the same reference format.
options.why: This removes the explicit governing instruction boundary and makes the policy harder to distinguish from evidence whose authority and effective period differ.

options.text: Separate bulletins as references with provenance; require conclusions to apply current rules to quoted facts.
options.why: Reference text remains available as evidence, but its quotations do not acquire instruction authority simply because the model can read them.

options.text: Identify current rules as instructions, explicitly stating that quoted historical procedures cannot override them.
options.why: The template explicitly states the authority relationship instead of forcing the model to infer policy precedence from whichever text appears most persuasive.

options.text: Label examples as illustrative, with effective policy versions and expected behavior distinct from live input.
options.why: This preserves useful historical examples while preventing their obsolete actions from silently becoming the current case's operating procedure.

options.text: Wrap the unchanged template in one trusted XML element, giving every statement corporate-instruction authority.
options.why: One outer delimiter preserves the original authority confusion; it does not distinguish current rules, historical examples, and quoted supplier procedures.

questions.decision: Give each section an explicit purpose and authority: current rules govern, examples illustrate, and source quotations supply evidence. Mark effective versions and require the answer to apply the governing policy. This structural repair improves interpretation; it remains a prompt-level measure and does not replace authorization checks at any consequential tool boundary.

video_evidence.concept: Tagged prompt sections separate roles, rules, output format, and reference data.

questions.title: Diversity must cover the failure slice
questions.stem: A metadata assistant trained only on monologues misattributes panel remarks and forces single-speaker output. Its schema already permits multiple speakers and unknown identity. Four examples can change before held-out evaluation. Which TWO changes address the generalization gap?

options.text: Remove unknown identity from the schema, requiring a named speaker for each turn to simplify comparison.
options.why: This removes the safe behavior already permitted for genuinely ambiguous evidence and encourages unsupported assignments instead of repairing the example coverage.

options.text: Increase reasoning with unchanged examples; treat improvements on those same examples as held-out validation.
options.why: Additional reasoning does not correct contradictory demonstrations, and evaluating the edited examples themselves cannot establish generalization to unseen panels.

options.text: Add adjudicated speaker switches and overlaps, using multi-speaker fields with textual evidence for assignments.
options.why: These demonstrate the structural behavior missing from the monologue-only examples and connect assignments to evidence rather than assuming a single participant.

options.text: Add four longer monologues on different topics, using topical variety to establish attribution diversity.
options.why: More topics do not expose speaker transitions or uncertainty, so the accidental single-speaker assumption remains demonstrated in every example.

options.text: Add ambiguous identities returning unknown; test unseen panels and ordinary monologues against one attribution rubric.
options.why: This teaches the permitted abstention boundary and tests whether the repair generalizes without losing the ordinary behavior the service still needs.

questions.decision: Replace redundant monologues with varied, adjudicated panel cases that demonstrate both multiple speakers and uncertainty. Preserve ordinary-task coverage and test unseen variants. Diversity matters because the examples currently teach a false structural assumption; adding volume or more deliberation would not correct that accidental lesson without changing the examples' decision coverage.

video_evidence.concept: Few-shot examples should be relevant and diverse rather than teaching an accidental narrow pattern.

questions.title: A schema migration still has failure paths
questions.stem: An app replaces assistant-prefix formatting with schema-constrained output on a supported Claude endpoint using output_config.format. Records need exactly three fields. Before writing, consumers must handle refusals and truncation. Which TWO choices complete the migration?

options.text: Describe three keys in user instructions; accept any parseable JSON as satisfying the field contract.
options.why: Parseability alone does not enforce required keys or additional-property rules, and an informal formatting instruction loses the selected constrained-output mechanism.

options.text: Configure JSON schema through output_config.format; verify required fields and additional-property behavior on the deployed endpoint.
options.why: This uses the documented constrained-output mechanism rather than relying on a token prefix or an informal request to approximate the required structure.

options.text: Keep the assistant prefix alongside schema mode, assuming both methods work across every model revision.
options.why: Support is endpoint- and model-specific; retaining an incompatible prefill can cause request errors rather than provide independent protection for the new schema path.

options.text: Write available fields after any HTTP success, treating schema mode as making stop reasons irrelevant.
options.why: Transport success does not establish complete usable output, and refusal or truncation must not become a partially committed business update.

options.text: Handle refusal and output-cap termination before consumption, then validate business values in completed objects.
options.why: Exceptional responses and semantic errors require consumer handling even when the normal output path is constrained to the declared JSON shape.

questions.decision: Use the supported schema mechanism and validate the response state before consuming the object. Constrained shape does not establish a valid business value, and documented exceptional stop states still need explicit handling. The chapter's migration lesson is extended here to the complete consumer contract rather than merely replacing a brace-prefill technique.

video_evidence.concept: Structured outputs replace brittle formatting techniques but do not eliminate refusal or truncation handling.

questions.title: Count after assembling what will be sent
questions.stem: A translation portal admits inputs below 48,000 tokens but counts only attachments before adding a glossary, tools, and scanned cover. Multilingual jobs exceed budget. A documented model-specific counting endpoint is available. Which design BEST aligns admission with the actual input?

options.text: Divide assembled characters by four; treat the result as exact across languages and scanned-image content.
options.why: Character ratios vary and do not represent all multimodal processing, so including text alone does not make that heuristic an exact model-specific count.

options.text: Reuse the previous input count for matching filenames, treating those names as equivalent request content.
options.why: A filename does not identify the full request or selected model, and changed glossary, tools, or image content can materially alter token use.

options.text: Assemble the final request, count supported content for the selected model, then admit with margin or reduce context.
options.why: The counting boundary now covers the payload actually sent and supports a conservative service budget rather than an incomplete attachment-only estimate.

options.text: Count attachments only; reserve a fixed output allowance to cover the appended glossary and tool inputs.
options.why: Output allowance does not cover glossary or tool input, so this continues excluding material that directly contributes to the request's input size.

questions.decision: Assemble and count the exact candidate request before admission, allowing a conservative margin for estimates and subsequent changes. Counted input and permitted output are separate quantities. Counting only the attachment misses the glossary, tools, and image representation that the model will actually receive, which explains the observed admission failure.

video_evidence.concept: Token counting should reflect the complete model-specific request, including multimodal and tool content.

questions.title: Cache lifetime follows request starts
questions.stem: Identical model/prefix requests use the default five-minute cache, which refreshes from qualifying request starts. No other traffic occurs. The first response streams for four minutes. Given the exhibit, which conclusion follows without extending cache lifetime from response completion?

options.text: Both later requests rewrite: entries expire at wall-clock five-minute marks, even with matching model and prefix.
options.why: Expiry follows the qualifying write or read start rather than a global wall-clock schedule, and the second request arrives within the initial lifetime.

options.text: Both later requests read: the initial four-minute response postpones the start of its cache lifetime.
options.why: Generation time counts against the lifetime; response completion does not postpone cache expiry or provide an additional unused five-minute period.

options.text: The 12:04:40 request rewrites: reads cannot refresh the default cache once its initial write completes.
options.why: The documented default cache refreshes on use, so a qualifying request before expiry can extend the lifetime without rewriting the cached prefix.

options.text: The 12:09:55 request misses: the 12:04:40 read refreshed expiry to 12:09:40, independent of response completion.
options.why: The five-minute lifetime starts at the last qualifying request start, making the final gap five minutes fifteen seconds rather than less than five.

questions.decision: The 12:04:40 read refreshes the entry through 12:09:40. The next request starts at 12:09:55, fifteen seconds too late, so it needs a new write under these stated conditions. Streaming completion does not move the deadline. This timing calculation extends the chapter's steady-traffic lesson to an actual quiet gap.

video_evidence.concept: Cache reads refresh the TTL; lifetime is measured from the start of the writing or reading request.

questions.title: A reference needs a discoverable entry point
questions.stem: An incident-response skill embeds twenty device-family tables; each incident needs one, and unrelated tasks invoke the same agent. The runtime supports metadata, instructions, and references. Which design BEST reduces irrelevant context while preserving table discovery and the mandatory recovery sequence?

options.text: Move all tables into the system prompt; minimize the skill body to reduce incident-related request context.
options.why: Moving the same tables into always-loaded instructions retains their context cost and makes unrelated work carry the entire incident reference collection.

options.text: Move tables and the mandatory sequence to one unlabelled file; retain only a general skill description.
options.why: This reduces initial text but removes the selection and workflow guidance needed to discover the right procedure and preserve its mandatory ordering.

options.text: Create a skill per table and insert every complete skill body at each session's start.
options.why: Preloading every complete skill defeats the proposed context economy and exposes unrelated procedures on tasks that do not require incident recovery.

options.text: Keep the sequence and family-selection map in the body; load named, versioned family references on demand.
options.why: The entry point retains task guidance and reliable navigation while loading only the applicable detailed table rather than every family's material.

questions.decision: Keep selection guidance and mandatory sequence in the skill body, with clearly named family references loaded only when relevant. Moving content out is insufficient if the entry point no longer tells the agent what to load. The chapter's progressive-disclosure lesson here includes preserving the retrieval path and version relationship needed for correct execution.

video_evidence.concept: Skills use progressive disclosure: concise entry instructions and reference material loaded when needed.

questions.title: Discovery does not revoke capability
questions.stem: A campus assistant needs room hours and amenities. Its registry also exposes locks, staff schedules, and alarm resets from a pilot. Deferred discovery shrinks prompts but still reveals alarm reset. Facilities denies this assistant operational authority. Which change BEST enforces its role?

options.text: Rank alarm resets below room information in discovery, retaining the registry because relevant tools usually appear first.
options.why: Ranking changes likelihood of selection but does not remove the control capability discovered in the red-team case or enforce the stated role boundary.

options.text: Remove controls and staff schedules from its authorized registry; retain the scoped room-information operations it needs.
options.why: This withdraws out-of-role behavior rather than hiding definitions, while preserving the read capabilities necessary to answer room-information questions.

options.text: Retain the registry and review alarm resets weekly, using accountability to enforce the assistant's information-only role.
options.why: Review can identify misuse after execution, but the facilities owner has stated that this assistant must not possess the capability at all.

options.text: Expose every tool during discovery so the model can compare all descriptions before choosing a room-information operation.
options.why: More visible definitions may assist comparison but increase context and leave the unauthorized operational-control role intact rather than minimizing capability.

questions.decision: Remove the out-of-role operations from the assistant's reachable registry and authorization scope. Deferred loading can still optimize legitimate information tools, but cannot establish least privilege while disallowed operations remain discoverable. This applies the chapter's capability-bloat principle to a catalog that appears smaller only because its definitions load later.

video_evidence.concept: Capability bloat requires removing irrelevant authority; deferred discovery alone only changes loaded context.

questions.title: Inspect effective subagent tools
questions.stem: An audit-only Claude Code subagent omits tools, so documented behavior inherits the parent's edit and shell tools. A maintainer wants it reviewing untrusted pull requests. Which TWO measures establish and verify read-only capability before enabling that workflow?

options.text: Ban one write command in examples; use a write-free happy-path run as proof of read-only capability.
options.why: A happy-path absence of use does not establish absence of capability, and examples do not define the full inherited tool boundary.

options.text: Verify in a controlled workflow that edit and execution requests are unavailable under the actual parent configuration.
options.why: Effective-state verification tests the deployed inheritance boundary rather than assuming that the configuration file's presence guarantees the intended runtime exposure.

options.text: Retain omitted tools; strengthen the role description and system instruction to revoke inherited tool access.
options.why: Instructions can guide behavior but do not revoke inherited tools; the stated runtime contract requires an explicit list to constrain that exposure.

options.text: Give it an isolated context while retaining inherited tools, treating isolation as making shell commands read-only.
options.why: A separate context limits information sharing, not external tool authority, so inherited shell or edit capabilities remain available to the subagent.

options.text: Explicitly allow supported read/search tools in its definition, excluding mutation and shell execution capabilities.
options.why: An explicit tools field replaces the inherited broad set with capabilities aligned to the audit role instead of relying on descriptive wording.

questions.decision: Specify the audit role's supported read tools and verify its resolved tool exposure in the actual workflow. A description states intent, while configuration determines inherited capability. This extends the chapter's configuration fix through an effective-state check so parent permissions and deployment differences cannot silently undo the intended read-only role.

video_evidence.concept: An omitted subagent tools field inherits tools; an explicit allowed-tool list limits the role.

questions.title: Bind an authorization code and its destination
questions.stem: An MCP desktop client uses two remote HTTP servers sharing an identity provider. A catalogue token works at instrument control; another client instance can redeem a captured code. Both use TLS. Which TWO client behaviors address these failures, alongside required server validation?

options.text: Use the required PKCE challenge and verifier to bind code redemption to the initiating client instance.
options.why: PKCE addresses interception or redemption of an authorization code by a different party, rather than relying solely on the transport connection's confidentiality.

options.text: Give servers distinct display names and rely on TLS to establish each access token's target resource.
options.why: Display labels and transport encryption do not bind an intercepted code to its initiator or prove that an access token was issued for a particular server.

options.text: Share one token across servers when issuer and user match, reducing consent prompts and token exchanges.
options.why: Shared issuer and identity do not establish the same intended audience, and token reuse would preserve the destination-confusion failure in the scenario.

options.text: Send the intended server's resource indicator in authorization and token requests to scope the requested credential.
options.why: The resource parameter identifies the destination for which the credential is requested; the receiving server must also reject tokens issued for another audience.

options.text: Expose tokens in tool descriptions, letting the model select the credential appropriate for each server call.
options.why: The client should handle credentials outside model context, and model selection of tokens does not provide protocol binding of code redemption or intended audience.

questions.decision: Use PKCE to bind code redemption to the initiating client and send the intended MCP resource indicator in authorization and token requests. These address different boundaries. The resource server must still validate tokens for its own audience; TLS and shared issuer trust cannot turn a token for another service into valid authority here.

video_evidence.concept: HTTP MCP authorization requires PKCE and resource indicators for the intended server.

questions.title: Keep the quality-critical prefix intact
questions.stem: An export-control explainer repeatedly sends an approved manual before case questions. Time to first token is the bottleneck. Smaller models fail exception tests; trimming the manual removes required clauses. Prefix caching is supported. Which optimization BEST preserves tested quality?

options.text: Cache the stable manual before case content; measure warm and cold first-token latency under representative traffic.
options.why: This attacks repeated prefix processing while preserving the tested model and necessary evidence, with measurements that expose actual cache reuse and cold-path behavior.

options.text: Increase reasoning to improve answer confidence, treating more confident completion as evidence of lower initial latency.
options.why: More reasoning does not eliminate repeated prefix processing, and confidence is not a measurement of the user's time-to-first-token bottleneck.

options.text: Delete infrequent exception clauses before requests, treating their low usage as sufficient to retain prior quality results.
options.why: Removing required evidence changes the tested configuration and directly undermines the exception cases that established the manual's required scope.

options.text: Switch to the smaller model and report median latency, excluding the uncommon exception cases it fails.
options.why: The candidate already fails required quality tests, and excluding that slice hides the known regression rather than making the latency trade-off acceptable.

questions.decision: Reuse processing of the stable manual prefix and measure cache reads and time to first token on representative traffic. This preserves the evidence and evaluated model configuration. Caching is an optimization hypothesis with observable usage, not a promise that all latency disappears; cold requests and changing content still need their own service measurements.

video_evidence.concept: Cache stable repeated context before sacrificing quality to reduce time to first token.

questions.title: An ensemble must fit the whole envelope
questions.stem: An invoice extractor requires ≥97% accuracy, p95 ≤4 seconds, and cost ≤0.12 units/document. The exhibit measures complete paths, including a concurrent three-pass vote, on representative workload. Which release decision meets all three gates?

options.text: Select the verifier: the most accurate configuration remains eligible whenever its document cost stays within budget.
options.why: The verifier meets quality and cost but exceeds the four-second p95 requirement, making it ineligible under the stated release contract.

options.text: Run the votes sequentially but retain the parallel p95, because scheduling changes cost rather than elapsed time.
options.why: Changing scheduling creates a different latency path, so the parallel measurements cannot justify the same completion claim for sequential execution.

options.text: Select the parallel vote: its measured accuracy, end-to-end p95, and cost pass; continue monitoring the configuration.
options.why: All three requirements hold simultaneously in the measured configuration, so the additional voting cost is justified within the explicitly permitted budget.

options.text: Select the single pass: its cost and speed advantages compensate for narrowly missing the mandatory accuracy floor.
options.why: Independent hard gates do not compensate for one another; the single pass fails quality even though it has useful speed and cost advantages.

questions.decision: Release the three-pass vote under the stated evidence: 97.4%, 3.6 seconds, and 0.105 units meet every gate. The single pass misses quality, while the verifier path misses latency despite its higher accuracy. These observations support this workload-specific choice, not a general assertion that concurrency eliminates latency or that extra samples guarantee correctness.

video_evidence.concept: A measured accuracy-latency-cost trade-off can justify parallel voting when all constraints hold.

questions.title: Sampling needs coverage and correlation
questions.stem: A permit assistant serves millions daily. Operators need tenant regression detection, tool-failure diagnosis, and slow-request reconstruction. Raw permit documents are unapproved for routine tracing. Beyond a random 1% trace sample, which THREE additions preserve visibility within those limits?

options.text: Retain failed and unusually slow runs within explicit capacity limits; alert when diagnostic retention drops data.
options.why: Exception-aware capture prioritizes the paths operators need, while visible overflow prevents an unrealistic promise to retain unlimited diagnostic events during an incident.

options.text: Retain only the first 1% of daily requests; treat their errors as representative across tenants and times.
options.why: A time-ordered early sample can miss tenant or load changes later in the day and does not provide population denominators or exception coverage.

options.text: Correlate retrieval, model, and tool spans using identifiers, permitted versions, and statuses rather than raw documents.
options.why: Sanitized correlated spans support reconstruction across stages without violating the scenario's unapproved raw-document tracing boundary.

options.text: Keep counts and latency distributions for all requests by approved tenant and release IDs, retaining rate denominators.
options.why: Population metrics reveal broad regressions and support rates even when only a fraction of individual request traces is retained for detailed investigation.

options.text: Keep complete successful sample payloads and discard failed traces, reserving diagnostic storage for usable final answers.
options.why: Failed paths are central diagnostic evidence, and routine full payload retention also conflicts with the explicit content boundary for permit documents.

questions.decision: Keep population-level counters, retain diagnostic exceptions, and correlate sanitized traces across stages. Random sampling alone can miss rare consequential failures and lacks complete denominators. This extends the chapter's scale strategy with explicit privacy and causal linkage: detailed traces should be purposeful, while aggregate metrics preserve coverage of the full service.

video_evidence.concept: At scale retain broad metrics and sampled traces with important error and anomalous paths preserved.

questions.title: Overlap is an indexing obligation
questions.stem: An oral-history exporter supplies timestamps but no reliable headings. Non-overlapping token windows lose anecdotes at chunk edges. Editors need citations opening relevant recording segments. Which indexing revision BEST addresses the observed failure using available source structure?

options.text: Index whole recordings, treating removal of token cuts as guaranteed evidence precision and sufficient citation granularity.
options.why: Whole recordings avoid cuts but can overwhelm context and reduce ranking precision, and they do not inherently satisfy the requested segment-level citation behavior.

options.text: Test bounded overlapping windows on edge-spanning anecdotes, retaining source and time offsets for recording-segment citations.
options.why: This directly supplies context across observed cut points while preserving the precise source navigation required for usable recording citations.

options.text: Index isolated sentences without timestamps, treating shorter retrieval units as sufficient context for complete anecdotes.
options.why: An anecdote may depend on neighboring sentences, and discarding timestamps removes the required path to the relevant recording segment.

options.text: Generate chapter headings and trust them as source boundaries without checking against the original spoken narrative.
options.why: Generated headings add derived structure whose accuracy is unproven; assuming their authority does not address the observed boundary failure with reliable evidence.

questions.decision: Use bounded overlapping windows and retain recording offsets for citations, then test whether boundary cases recover their evidence. Overlap is not a universal chunk size prescription; it addresses this exporter and observed failure pattern. Generated topic headings may become useful metadata after validation, but should not be treated as source structure that does not exist.

video_evidence.concept: Fixed-size chunks with overlap suit unstructured prose and preserve boundary-spanning ideas.

questions.title: Embedding is a separate dependency
questions.stem: An archive assumes Messages supplies 'Claude embeddings'; documentation says Anthropic has no embedding model. Specialist abbreviations need testing, and outbound routes need approval. Which TWO changes make the dependency explicit without assuming a recommended provider fits?

options.text: Evaluate embedding candidates on archive-specific relevance and query latency before choosing corpus/query encoding settings.
options.why: Provider availability does not establish local retrieval quality; specialist abbreviations require direct measurements under the archive's actual query and latency requirements.

options.text: Retain the Claude embeddings box and add a vector database to create compatible corpus/query representations.
options.why: A vector store holds or searches representations; adding it does not establish a supported service for producing the required compatible embeddings.

options.text: Adopt the documentation's example provider, treating that example as approval for all outbound archive-data routes.
options.why: A first-party example does not authorize the organization's data transfers or demonstrate that the candidate meets specialist corpus and query requirements.

options.text: Specify a supported embedding service with credentials, processing route, and corpus-index ownership in the architecture.
options.why: The design now represents a real supported capability and makes its independent security and data-processing boundary reviewable instead of hiding it inside generation.

options.text: Generate numeric lists through Messages as drop-in vectors, avoiding a separate embedding-provider assessment and contract.
options.why: Generated numeric text is not a documented embedding API with a stable retrieval contract, so it does not repair the unsupported architectural dependency.

questions.decision: Add an actual embedding service with an approved data path, and evaluate its retrieval behavior on the archive's queries. Claude generation does not silently supply corpus vectors. The provider described in documentation is a candidate rather than an automatic winner; specialist language, latency, and processing constraints still determine whether the complete retrieval design is suitable.

video_evidence.concept: Generation and embedding are separate capabilities; select and evaluate an actual embedding provider.

questions.title: Rank only eligible reservations
questions.stem: A room request requires wheelchair access, capacity ≥18, and availability on the booking date. Authoritative structured fields hold these constraints. Descriptions capture preferences such as quiet settings. Which retrieval strategy BEST combines eligibility with semantic relevance?

options.text: Search descriptions for 'eighteen' and 'wheelchair,' treating those words as equivalent to current eligibility fields.
options.why: Keyword mentions can refer to historical, comparative, or unrelated facts and cannot substitute for authoritative eligibility and current booking data.

options.text: Retrieve five nearest descriptions, inferring accessibility and capacity whenever their narratives suit the requested meeting.
options.why: Narrative similarity does not enforce structured predicates, so highly ranked descriptions can still violate the explicit room requirements.

options.text: Filter authoritative eligibility fields, then semantically rank eligible rooms for the setting and explain supporting evidence.
options.why: Hard constraints define the candidate set while semantic retrieval orders valid options for a preference that is expressed descriptively rather than as an exact field.

options.text: Rank all descriptions and add an availability disclaimer, allowing ineligible suggestions because no reservation happens yet.
options.why: A disclaimer does not satisfy the explicit recommendation constraints, which require eligible options even before the separate act of making a reservation.

questions.decision: Apply the hard predicates to authoritative fields and rank eligible spaces by meaning. Preserve eligibility through pagination and any final availability check. Similarity is useful for quiet-setting preferences, but it cannot prove capacity, accessibility, or current booking availability. The complete query must respect both the structured constraints and the descriptive relevance objective.

video_evidence.concept: Use structured constraints for hard predicates and semantic ranking for descriptive preferences.

questions.title: A connector subset is an interface boundary
questions.stem: A Messages app's MCP connector supports tools, not resources. A permission-checked, versioned collection guide exists only as a resource on its public HTTP server. Which TWO paths can legitimately supply it within this interface boundary?

options.text: With server-owner approval, expose a scoped guide-read tool retaining access checks and version metadata.
options.why: A genuine tool interface can fit the supported connector subset while preserving the resource's authorization and provenance obligations through the new operation.

options.text: Increase cache lifetime and submit the resource URI as instructions, treating expiration as blocking resource discovery.
options.why: Caching changes reuse of supplied context, not the connector's protocol feature support, so this cannot implement a resource operation it does not expose.

options.text: Disable server tools so the connector falls back to resources as its next available protocol capability.
options.why: Removing supported tools does not create unsupported resource operations or establish a new permission-checked content assembly path.

options.text: Switch the server to local stdio but retain remote connector configuration to unlock missing MCP features.
options.why: The connector's documented transport and feature boundaries remain relevant; an unsupported transport is not a solution for a missing resource capability.

options.text: Use an application-owned, resource-capable MCP client; read authorized content and assemble its version into the request.
options.why: The application handles the unsupported protocol feature explicitly and controls which authorized resource content becomes model context.

questions.decision: Use a resource-capable application client, or intentionally expose an authorized read operation as a tool when that interface fits the server. Both require provenance and access control. A connector's support for one MCP feature does not imply every protocol feature is supported, and cache lifetime cannot add a missing resource-read mechanism.

video_evidence.concept: The Messages MCP connector supports a subset of MCP, including tools rather than direct resource use.

questions.title: A deterministic transaction need not be a delegation
questions.stem: One app submits approved purchase orders to an existing API. Fields, retryable errors, and idempotency behavior are specified; submission needs no interpretation. Which design BEST preserves approved-order identity and recovery from uncertain responses?

options.text: Have a coding assistant run the procurement CLI per production order, keeping only its conversation as the submission record.
options.why: An interactive development conversation is not the durable production transaction identity and explicit recovery contract that this already specified API operation requires.

options.text: Delegate orders to an agent choosing parameters and retries from general approval guidance.
options.why: The execution parameters are already fixed, so introducing agent discretion weakens rather than fulfills the requirement for controlled approved-order submission.

options.text: Publish a general purchasing MCP server, using successful discovery as evidence that uncertain responses reconcile safely.
options.why: MCP discovery does not implement transaction reconciliation, and the stated workload does not require a shared discovery interface before submission can be controlled.

options.text: Use an application adapter with durable order IDs, explicit idempotency keys, and documented reconciliation and retry rules.
options.why: This matches the fully specified operation and keeps recovery of uncertain outcomes under deterministic application control rather than model interpretation.

questions.decision: Use the existing API through application code with durable order identity and the provider's documented recovery behavior. There is no unresolved reasoning task for a delegated agent and no multi-client discovery requirement demanding an MCP layer. Those interfaces could be useful elsewhere, but their additional machinery supplies no missing requirement in this transaction path.

video_evidence.concept: Direct APIs fit tightly controlled deterministic integration when shared agent discovery adds no requirement.

questions.title: Deferred discovery must preserve prefix identity
questions.stem: An agent uses tool search and a cached policy. It rebuilds initial tool definitions after each discovery and inserts changing session labels before the cache breakpoint. Supported discovery instead returns definitions through conversation. Which TWO changes improve reuse?

options.text: Stop measuring cache creation; use lower average token bills to prove discovery leaves the prefix unchanged.
options.why: A total bill has multiple drivers and cannot isolate prefix reuse, while omitting creation usage removes evidence needed to diagnose cache misses.

options.text: Keep deferred definitions in the documented tool-search result flow, preserving the initial cached tool/policy prefix.
options.why: This preserves the supported append behavior instead of introducing application changes that unnecessarily alter the reusable initial request prefix.

options.text: Move session labels past the cache boundary; compare read/creation usage with identical policy and model versions.
options.why: The changing label is an independent prefix mismatch, and usage measurements establish whether both repairs produce actual reuse rather than merely configured caching.

options.text: Keep rebuilding tools and labels but extend TTL, making different prefixes refer to the same cached content.
options.why: TTL extends lifetime for matching content; it does not make a changed tools array or session label identical to an already cached prefix.

options.text: Preload all tools, assuming every discovery result invalidates prior cached tokens regardless of conversation representation.
options.why: The documentation describes a compatible discovery path; the proposed universal invalidation assumption would discard its context economy without addressing the changing session label.

questions.decision: Use the documented discovery flow and keep request-varying labels outside the reusable prefix. Then inspect actual cache usage to distinguish tool changes from other prefix changes. The chapter rejects an inherent conflict between discovery and caching; this scenario adds the important qualification that application-side rewriting can still destroy otherwise reusable prefix identity.

video_evidence.concept: Discovered tools can be appended without invalidating an unchanged cached prefix.

questions.title: Security rates need adversarial denominators
questions.stem: A dispatch assistant reads restricted records and drafts external messages. Existing metrics cover answer quality, latency, and cost. Staging permits labeled adversarial tests with synthetic data. Which TWO measurements directly test resistance to injected disclosure and unauthorized tool use?

options.text: Measure attempted and executed out-of-scope actions separately against the staging account's explicit permissions under injection.
options.why: Separating requests from execution distinguishes model behavior from enforced containment and directly measures whether the intended capability boundary holds.

options.text: Measure restricted content reaching external drafts using canary records, with the number of adversarial attempts as denominator.
options.why: This directly tests the confidentiality outcome instead of inferring it from citation presence, response fluency, or transport status.

options.text: Measure ordinary scheduling helpfulness, treating score increases as evidence of stronger resistance to retrieved hostile instructions.
options.why: Ordinary helpfulness does not test prohibited disclosure or tool authority, and it can remain high while an adversarial security boundary fails.

options.text: Measure attack-input tokens, treating larger contexts containing more restriction text as evidence of greater safety.
options.why: Token volume measures resource use, not whether the tested confidentiality and action boundaries actually resist hostile content.

options.text: Count HTTP-success attack responses as security passes, assuming all authority violations cause network or transport failures.
options.why: Security failures can occur inside successful requests, so HTTP status cannot establish whether content was disclosed or a tool action exceeded authority.

questions.decision: Add explicit disclosure and unauthorized-action outcomes with declared attack denominators and expected permissions. These reveal whether the system violates security boundaries, even when requests complete normally and answers look fluent. Staging and synthetic data make the evaluation controlled; a clean result remains evidence for the tested attacks, not proof of universal resistance.

video_evidence.concept: Measure data leakage and unauthorized tool behavior directly under adversarial inputs.

questions.title: Measure first usable text at the agreed edge
questions.stem: A streaming model emits its first token at 0.6 seconds; proxy buffering adds two seconds before users see text. The owner wants visible-answer start time and separate completion latency. Which measurement BEST captures that experience and locates the delay?

options.text: Measure browser request-to-visible-text time; keep model first-token and full completion timings to locate the delay.
options.why: This observes the user-relevant start of visible text and retains component evidence needed to diagnose why model emission does not reach the browser promptly.

options.text: Measure average output length instead, treating shorter answers as starting to render earlier through the same proxy.
options.why: Output length may affect completion time but does not identify when buffering releases initial content or when the browser first renders answer text.

options.text: Report provider first-token percentiles only, treating downstream buffering as affecting completion but not perceived response start.
options.why: Buffering directly delays visible text, so provider emission alone understates the experience that the service owner wants to measure.

options.text: Count successful stream connections as timely starts, even when only headers arrive and answer text remains buffered.
options.why: A connected stream can carry no visible answer text, so connection success does not measure the user's requested response-start experience.

questions.decision: Instrument request start to the first rendered answer text at the browser, alongside upstream first-token and completion spans. The provider's early token does not bypass proxy buffering. This extends the chapter's perceived-latency lesson by making the measurement edge explicit: the correct metric must observe the moment that the intended user actually experiences.

video_evidence.concept: Track time to first token alongside end-to-end time for streamed perceived latency.

questions.title: A swapped verdict is not missing at random
questions.stem: A pairwise judge favors the first summary on difficult cases. The proposed fix drops order-inconsistent pairs and generalizes the remainder's win rate to all cases. Experts can adjudicate a subset; difficult cases matter for release. Which TWO changes improve validity?

options.text: Test both orders with blinded identities; retain order-specific verdicts and report the fraction changed by swapping.
options.why: Counterbalancing exposes positional sensitivity and preserves the evidence needed to distinguish stable preferences from a judge's presentation dependence.

options.text: Adjudicate representative inconsistent pairs and report their coverage separately, limiting consistent-subset claims to that subset.
options.why: This addresses difficult-case exclusion and makes the judge's unresolved coverage visible rather than silently generalizing from an easier selected subset.

options.text: Drop inconsistent pairs and multiply the remainder's win rate by the full dataset size to estimate improvements.
options.why: Scaling a selected subset does not repair selection bias; inconsistent cases may systematically represent the difficult decisions that matter for release.

options.text: Always place the incumbent second, using first-position preference to offset its existing advantage in production.
options.why: Fixed placement substitutes another systematic bias for the original one and cannot reveal which verdicts depend on presentation order.

options.text: Show candidate names and request longer explanations, treating persuasive reasoning as evidence that order effects are harmless.
options.why: Longer explanations and visible identity do not establish order invariance, and candidate identity can introduce additional preference unrelated to answer quality.

questions.decision: Counterbalance order and retain inconsistent outcomes as a visible category for adjudication or separate reporting. Discarding them may disproportionately remove difficult tasks and change the estimand. The video suggests consistent verdicts; this novel extension qualifies that shortcut so the result does not silently become a claim about a population the judge failed to cover.

video_evidence.concept: Counterbalance pairwise presentation to expose position bias; do not mistake consistent subsets for unbiased population estimates.

questions.title: Scale grading at the right boundaries
questions.stem: Shipping-note evaluation covers exact container IDs and semantic exception explanations. Experts can grade sixty cases weekly. Code can check IDs; a rubric judge can be calibrated for support. Which design BEST expands coverage while retaining expert authority over ambiguous exceptions?

options.text: Use an uncalibrated judge for every field; treat its larger case count as more trustworthy than expert grading.
options.why: Volume does not establish grader validity, and automating exact fields through an unvalidated semantic judge adds unnecessary uncertainty to an objectively checkable property.

options.text: Exact-match IDs and explanations alike, marking any paraphrase of an approved handling exception as incorrect.
options.why: Exact identifiers fit code checks, but legitimate semantic paraphrases need a support rubric; string equality would measure wording rather than explanation correctness.

options.text: Limit evaluation to sixty expert cases, excluding automated checks even for identifiers with documented expected values.
options.why: Human authority is valuable, but excluding reliable code checks needlessly limits broad regression coverage on fields that already have an objective oracle.

options.text: Check IDs with code and explanations with a calibrated judge; expand coverage with expert audits of consequential disagreements.
options.why: Each method addresses a property it can assess, while targeted human oversight checks the automated grader rather than disappearing from the evaluation process.

questions.decision: Grade exact fields with code and explanation support with a calibrated judge, reserving expert time for calibration, ambiguity, and important disagreements. Scale increases coverage only if the grader measures the right property. The chapter's automation preference is qualified here: many automated cases with an unvalidated judge do not automatically outrank a small trustworthy assessment.

video_evidence.concept: Use scalable code and calibrated model grading where appropriate, with human calibration and targeted review.

questions.title: Randomize at the shared learning boundary
questions.stem: A tutoring trial compares feedback styles. Pupils influence each other through group lessons, so pupil assignment still permits classroom spillover; message assignment also mixes personal exposure. Enough classrooms support a cluster trial. Which TWO changes align assignment and analysis?

options.text: Analyze with classroom clustering and report independent classroom counts, retaining pupil data without treating messages as randomized units.
options.why: The assignment creates cluster dependence, so uncertainty and sample-size claims must reflect independent classrooms rather than inflate evidence through repeated messages.

options.text: Randomize messages and average by pupil afterward, treating aggregation as removing mixed instruction and classroom spillover.
options.why: Averaging does not reverse treatment contamination or classroom spillover caused by inconsistent exposure during the study.

options.text: Randomize pupils within classrooms and ignore group lessons because assistant conversations remain private between pupils.
options.why: The scenario explicitly states a shared teaching mechanism, so private chats alone do not establish absence of interference across pupil assignments.

options.text: Switch all classrooms at midday without a crossover plan, using time-of-day differences as evidence of fair balance.
options.why: Unplanned switching can confound exposure with time and carryover, and does not provide the stable, interpretable cluster comparison described in the requirement.

options.text: Assign each classroom one style consistently; predefine the exposure period and policy for safety interventions.
options.why: Class-level consistency addresses both within-pupil switching and the stated classroom spillover rather than treating every message as an independent exposure.

questions.decision: Use stable classroom assignment and account for classrooms as clusters in the analysis. This is a novel extension of the video's conversation-level consistency lesson: here interactions cross conversations through teaching, so the assignment boundary must cover that interference. Repeated messages add observations, but they do not create independent randomized classrooms.

video_evidence.concept: The randomization unit should match the experience, preventing arm contamination across related interactions.

questions.title: Abstain on a missing effective edition
questions.stem: A standards assistant answers a 2024 question using the 2026 edition, which changed the numerical limit. Its prompt demands a decisive answer and citation. Which repair BEST prevents unsupported edition claims while allowing answers when the right edition is available?

options.text: Increase output allowance for a fuller explanation of the 2026 limit while retaining its claimed 2024 applicability.
options.why: More explanation does not supply the missing edition or remove the unsupported assertion that a newer limit applied during the requested earlier period.

options.text: Require edition-matched support; disclose missing evidence and offer retrieval or escalation when only inapplicable editions appear.
options.why: This removes the instruction pressure to invent coverage and distinguishes a relevant-looking citation from evidence that supports the requested effective period.

options.text: Remove edition metadata from retrieval so the model no longer encounters conflicting procedure years in context.
options.why: Hiding applicability metadata makes the error harder to detect and encourages the same unsupported claim instead of establishing adequate evidence.

options.text: Retain mandatory decisive answers but emphasize the newer citation so readers can notice its different effective year.
options.why: A prominent citation does not make the 2026 number true for 2024 and leaves the known unsupported temporal inference in the final answer.

questions.decision: Require evidence that covers the requested effective edition and allow a documented no-answer state when it is absent. A citation is insufficient if it supports a different time scope. This applies the chapter's abstention lesson to a plausible but inapplicable source, rather than assuming that retrieved text always provides the answer requested.
